_meta: File paths that use different separators, used to show why splitting or joining paths with a hardcoded '/' breaks across operating systems and on data from another OS, and why path handling must use the library (which abstracts the separator) or account for both separators. The directory separator is OS-dependent: POSIX systems (Linux, macOS) use '/', and Windows uses '\\' (backslash), while also accepting '/'. Code that hardcodes one separator -- most commonly extracting a filename with path.split('/')[-1], or building a path with a + '/' + b -- works on the developer's machine and quietly fails elsewhere: it fails when the same code runs on the other OS, and it fails when the code processes a path string that originated on the other OS (an uploaded file, a path from a database, a cross-platform archive), even on the same machine. The tell is that a path containing a backslash, split on '/', comes back whole -- the split found no delimiter -- so the 'filename' is actually the entire path. The fix is to use the standard path library (os.path.basename / os.path.split, or pathlib.PurePath), which knows the platform separator and, for parsing foreign paths, to split on BOTH '/' and '\\'. paths is a list of path strings from mixed sources; expected is the correct filename (basename) of each. paths and expected are the fixture; the basename extracted by the naive '/'-split and by the separator-agnostic parse are computed.
